title: Drawing to Help Me Think
keyIdea: Putting words and a picture together helps you understand and remember. A thinking picture can be a quick sketch, a diagram with labels, or a timeline that shows what happens in order. It should be quick and simple, and show the idea, not decoration.

kid: You can draw to help you think. Draw a quick picture of the idea. It does not need to be neat or coloured in.
Add labels. A label is a word that names a part. Draw a plant and write roots, stem, leaf and flower.
A timeline shows things in order. Draw a seed, then roots, then a shoot, then a flower. Put arrows between them.
Words and a picture together give your brain two ways to remember. Keep it simple. Sparkles and rainbows look nice, but they do not help you think.
adult: This is dual coding: learning the same idea in words and in a picture. That gives two linked ways to recall it. The idea comes from Allan Paivio's dual coding theory. Richard Mayer's work on multimedia learning found that words with pictures that fit the idea beat words alone. Wammes, Meade and Fernandes (2016) found that drawing a word, even quickly, helped people remember it better than writing it out.

At 6 and 7 the useful forms are a quick sketch, a labelled diagram and a simple timeline or story map. In Year 1 science, children name the basic parts of flowering plants. By Years 3 and 4 they record findings with drawings and labelled diagrams. Timelines and story maps are used in KS1 history and English to put events in order. Talking while drawing helps, because the child links each part to a word.

Common mistakes: treating the drawing as an art task, so time goes on neat colouring instead of the idea; adding decoration that explains nothing (Mayer's coherence principle shows extra pictures can hurt learning); and leaving out the words, so the picture has no labels. Dual coding is not learning styles. Words plus pictures help every child, not just so-called visual learners.

In the lab your child makes a two-stamp sketch to show the sun above a tree, labels a plant diagram, adds pictures to word cards and uses a picture clue to find a word, puts seed, roots, shoot and flower into a timeline, and picks the picture that really explains an idea from three choices.

familyTip: After a story or a trip, ask your child to draw it in three boxes: first, next, last, with one or two words in each. When they learn something new, such as how a seed grows, say: draw it in one minute and label two parts. Then ask them to explain it to you using the drawing.

visual.caption: Does it help you think, or is it just decoration? Drag each card, or tap it and then tap a box.

items: A quick sketch of the idea

lab.caption: Flagship lab: make a quick sketch, label a plant, add pictures to word cards, build a seed-to-flower timeline and pick the picture that explains.

practice.prompt: You want to remember how a seed grows. What should you do?
choices: Draw it quickly and add labels
practice.hint: Think about words and a picture together, quick and simple.
practice.explain: A quick sketch with labels joins words and a picture, so you have two ways to remember it.

practice.prompt: Your plant drawing has {n} parts. You write one label on each part. How many labels do you write?
practice.hint: One label goes on each part. Count the parts.
practice.explain: One label for each part, and there are {n} parts, so you write {=n} labels.

practice.prompt: Your timeline has {n} boxes in a row. You draw an arrow between each box and the next one. How many arrows?
practice.hint: Arrows go between boxes. Count the gaps between the boxes, not the boxes.
practice.explain: {n} boxes in a row have {=n-1} gaps between them, so you draw {=n-1} arrows.

choices: A word that names a part
practice.hint: A label points to one part of a picture. What does it say?
practice.explain: A label is a short word that names a part, like roots or stem.

pool.prompt: Which picture would help you explain how rain makes a puddle?
choices: A cloud, rain and a puddle with arrows
pool.hint: Look for the picture that shows the idea in steps.
pool.explain: The cloud, rain and puddle with arrows show the steps. Glitter does not explain, and the car is about something else.

pool.prompt: How long should a thinking sketch take?
pool.hint: It is a quick picture to help you think, not an art show.
pool.explain: A thinking sketch is quick. A minute or two is enough to show the idea.

pool.prompt: Which shows things in the order they happen?
pool.hint: Look for the one that has first, next and last.
pool.explain: A timeline shows first, next and last. One picture shows only one moment.

pool.prompt: Why do a word and a picture help you remember?
choices: Your brain has two ways to find it
pool.hint: Think of the word path and the picture path.
pool.explain: A word and a picture give your brain two ways to find the idea again. Keep both.

pool.prompt: You draw {n} pictures for a story, one in each box. You add 1 word to each box. How many words do you write?
pool.hint: There is one word for each box. Count the boxes in your story.
pool.explain: There is 1 word for each of the {n} boxes, so you write {=n} words.

pool.prompt: Sam draws a fish with lots of sparkles but no labels. What would help most?
pool.hint: Which change helps someone learn the parts of a fish?
pool.explain: Labels name the parts, so they help you explain. Sparkles and colouring do not teach anything.

pool.prompt: A seed grows. Which comes first in the timeline?
pool.hint: Think about what you put in the soil at the start.
pool.explain: The seed comes first. Then roots, then a shoot, then a flower.

pool.prompt: Your friend asks how you get to school. What could you draw?
pool.hint: Pick the drawing that shows the way, step by step.
pool.explain: A quick map with arrows shows the way. You can point to it as you explain.

pool.prompt: You learn {n} new words. You draw a quick picture next to each word. How many pictures do you draw?
pool.hint: One quick picture goes with each word. Count the words.
pool.explain: One picture for each of the {n} words gives {=n} pictures, so each word has two ways in: the word and its picture.
